html:
The Caddo are a Native American people whose homeland lay in what is now northeast Texas, western Louisiana, southwest Arkansas and southeast Oklahoma. Today they form the Caddo Nation of Oklahoma.

Their ancestors were part of the Mississippian world (see Cahokia and Mississippian towns). From about 800 to 1400 CE they built large earthwork mounds at several sites in this country. They farmed maize, beans and squash in rich river bottoms and lived in tall grass houses.

The Caddo were organised in three confederacies: the Hasinai, Kadohadacho and Natchitoches. The Spanish called the Hasinai the Tejas, from a Caddo word for "friend", and that is where the name Texas comes from. Members of the de Soto expedition met Caddo peoples in 1542. In the late 1600s and 1700s Spain built missions among them to hold the land against the French of Louisiana (see New France), while the French traded with them from Natchitoches.

European diseases cut their numbers sharply. In the 1850s they were pushed onto a reservation in Texas, then removed to Indian Territory in 1859. Their relatives include the Wichita. Their western neighbours were the Tonkawa.
